analysis.one_liner: Bans TV and radio advertising of sports betting nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill banned advertising of sportsbooks on FCC-regulated media, but with only one cosponsor it never left a House subcommittee and received no vote before the session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Betting on Our Future Act would make it illegal to advertise sportsbooks — businesses that take sports bets — on any TV, radio, or other media regulated by the Federal Communications Commission. The goal is to cut down the flood of sports gambling ads that reaches viewers, including young people and people at risk of gambling addiction. It was introduced by Rep. Paul Tonko and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary viewers of broadcast TV and radio, especially young people and people vulnerable to gambling addiction, who would see far fewer sportsbook ads. Families affected by problem gambling would face less of the constant marketing that normalizes betting on every game.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to advertise a sportsbook on any medium of electronic communication under FCC jurisdiction, which covers broadcast TV and radio — removing sports betting ads from the mainstream airwaves.

The definition of a sports bet is written broadly, covering stakes on any sporting event and including fantasy or simulation sports contests, so the ad ban would reach the fast-growing fantasy betting market as well as traditional sportsbooks.

Enforcement runs through the Federal Communications Commission, treating a violation like any other breach of the Communications Act, so the regulator already overseeing broadcasters would police the ads without a new agency.

analysis.who_pays: Sports betting companies would lose their most visible advertising channel, and broadcast TV and radio stations plus leagues and networks would lose the ad revenue those dollars bring. Sportsbooks could still advertise on internet and social media platforms outside FCC jurisdiction, so the cost is a lost channel, not lost business entirely.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers only FCC-regulated media, so sportsbooks could keep advertising on podcasts, streaming apps, and social media — arguably where most young fans actually are — limiting the bill's real-world effect.
A flat prohibition on advertising a legal product raises free-speech concerns about restricting commercial speech, and it would not stop sports betting itself, only the ads for it.
Broadcasters, sports leagues, and media companies would lose advertising income, which some argue would simply shift costs onto fans through higher rights fees and subscription prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — fewer sports gambling ads aimed at a public facing a fast-growing betting market — is real but incomplete, since the bill leaves internet advertising untouched, which is where much of the spend has shifted. The cost falls on sportsbook marketing budgets and broadcaster revenue. On balance it is a modest consumer-protection measure with a real but narrow reach, and its bigger weakness was political: almost no other member of Congress signed on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the Betting on Our Future Act in the House on February 9, 2023, to ban sportsbook advertising on FCC-regulated media.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and a week later to the subcommittee handling communications and technology.
It picked up only one cosponsor in the entire two-year Congress — a single House Democrat — and no further action was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sports betting companies and the broadcasters, leagues, and media companies that sell their advertising came out ahead: they kept an unrestricted right to advertise on TV and radio for two more years while the bill sat untouched in committee.

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.role: Sponsor; House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed to ban sportsbook advertising on broadcast media.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Communications and Technology subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or vote on it in two years.

against.name: Sports betting industry
against.role: Sportsbook operators and their advertising partners
against.what_they_did: A legal sports betting market expanding nationwide had a direct financial stake in blocking a broadcast advertising ban; the bill died without reaching a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll-call record exists; both the sponsor and its sole cosponsor were House Democrats, and the Republican-led committee took no action.

industries.note: A ban on advertising over FCC-regulated media would cut sportsbooks off from broadcast TV and radio, their most visible marketing channel, right as legal sports betting was expanding across states. Their interest in running the ads runs against the public interest in limiting gambling marketing to young and at-risk viewers.

industries.industry: Broadcasters and sports media (TV and radio networks, leagues and teams that sell ad inventory)
industries.note: Stations and networks would lose the substantial ad dollars sportsbooks spend during games, and leagues and teams would lose sponsorship revenue tied to betting promotions.
Agencies and ad-tech firms serving sportsbook clients would lose a growing client category on broadcast channels, though work on internet ads would continue.
